key_terms.meaning: Fraction of fabricated chips that pass all tests; low yield raises test cost per good chip.
Physical imperfection in a chip, such as a short, open, or bad oxide.
Wrong logic value or timing at a circuit node caused by a defect.
Chip or system does not meet its specification because errors reach outputs.
Logical abstraction of a defect used by test software, such as a line stuck at 0.
A line behaves as if permanently 0 or 1; written stuck-at-0 or stuck-at-1.
A path or gate is too slow, so the correct value arrives after the clock edge.
Program that injects faults and counts how many are detected by a vector set.
Automatic test pattern generation: derives input vectors that detect chosen faults.
Detected faults divided by total faults in the fault list, often shown as a percentage.
Design style that connects flip-flops into shift registers for test.
All flip-flops are scan cells and are chained for test access.
Ease of setting an internal node to a desired 0 or 1 from primary inputs.
Ease of seeing an internal node value at primary outputs.
Test cells at chip pins let board wiring be tested through a serial port.
IEEE 1149.1 boundary-scan standard with TAP controller, TDI, TDO, TCK, and TMS.
Built-in self-test: on-chip pattern generator and response checker test the chip.
Ordered read/write sequence over memory addresses used to detect memory faults.
Die tested and certified before packaging or multichip assembly.
Quiescent supply current test; high current can reveal defects such as shorts.

takeaways: Testing compares each fabricated chip with its specification and controls how many bad chips reach the customer.
Fault models replace many physical defects with a small logical list that ATPG and fault simulation can handle.
Fault simulation measures fault coverage, while ATPG works backward from a fault to a detecting vector.
Scan design makes sequential test easier by shifting state in and out and treating the circuit as combinational during capture.
Boundary scan puts a test cell at every pin so board interconnect can be tested through a few serial wires.
BIST moves pattern generation and response checking on chip, reducing dependence on an external tester.
Memories need march algorithms because cell coupling and address decoder faults are not caught by simple stuck-at vectors.
Chip, package, board, and system test are separate stages that must be planned together for quality and cost.
Analog and mixed-signal blocks are tested by measuring specifications such as INL, DNL, gain, offset, SNR, and SINAD against tolerances.
bank_note: Long answers usually combine fault models with DFT methods: scan, JTAG, BIST, memory march tests, and the test flow from chip to board.

bank.q: Explain why every fabricated chip is tested and how manufacturing yield affects test cost and customer quality.
outline: Test compares chip behavior with specification.
Yield is good chips divided by total chips.
Low yield raises test cost per good chip.
Escapes cause field failures and warranty cost.
Test cost includes tester time and pin count.

bank.q: Define defect, error, failure, and fault. Explain why fault models are needed.
outline: Defect is physical imperfection.
Error is wrong logic value or timing.
Failure is specification violation.
Fault is logical abstraction for test software.
Fault models enable ATPG and fault simulation.

bank.q: Explain scan design. Define full scan, controllability, and observability.
outline: Scan cell adds a multiplexer before each flip-flop.
Shift mode forms a chain; capture mode tests logic.
Full scan means all flip-flops are scan cells.
Controllability is ease of setting internal nodes.
Observability is ease of seeing internal nodes at outputs.

bank.q: Describe boundary scan and the JTAG TAP controller.
outline: Boundary-scan cell sits at each chip pin.
TAP controller is a state machine driven by TMS and TCK.
Instruction register selects test mode.
Data registers include boundary-scan register and bypass.
Board wires are tested through daisy-chained TDI and TDO.

bank.q: Explain BIST architecture with a pattern generator and a response analyzer.
outline: On-chip generator applies test patterns.
LFSR or ROM can generate patterns.
Response analyzer compacts outputs into a signature.
Signature is compared with expected value.
BIST reduces external tester needs but has area and aliasing cost.

bank.q: A combinational circuit has a stuck-at-0 fault on one gate input. Explain step by step how ATPG derives a test vector that detects it.
outline: Activate fault by setting the faulty line to 1.
Propagate the error to an output through sensitive gates.
Justify required values back to primary inputs.
Check for conflicts; if none, vector is valid.
Good and faulty circuits must give different outputs.

bank.q: A full-scan design has 200 flip-flops. Find the shift cycles for one scan chain and for four equal scan chains, ignoring capture cycles.
outline: One chain needs 200 shift cycles.
Four chains need 50 shift cycles each.
Use N_ff divided by number of chains.
Capture cycles are extra.
More chains reduce shift time but need more pins or compression.

bank.q: A memory array is tested with a march algorithm. Explain how a march element such as rising(r0,w1) is applied and why address order matters.
outline: March element applies read and write steps at each address.
Rising order goes from low to high address.
r0 checks cell reads 0; w1 writes 1.
Order helps catch address decoder and coupling faults.
Complexity is linear in memory size.

bank.q: A board has four JTAG chips in a daisy chain. Explain how boundary scan tests a wire between two chip pins.
outline: Load EXTEST instruction into the chips.
Shift values into boundary-scan cells to drive the pin.
Capture the value at the receiving pin.
Shift out and compare with expected value.
Detects open and short board wires without a bed of nails.

bank.q: Explain how test compression reduces tester time and pin count in a scan design.
outline: On-chip decompressor expands few tester channels to many scan chains.
Compactor reduces many outputs to few.
More scan chains shorten shift length.
Tester memory and time fall.
Design needs compression logic and compatible scan chains.

bank.q: Compare stuck-at fault testing and delay fault testing. Why do delay faults need at-speed test?
outline: Stuck-at faults are static logic faults.
Delay faults are timing faults.
Transition or path test launches and captures at speed.
Slow tester can miss late-arriving values.
At-speed test needs fast clocking and careful timing.

bank.q: Evaluate full scan, partial scan, and BIST for a large SoC with reused IP blocks.
outline: Full scan gives high coverage but costs area and test time.
Partial scan reduces area but may lower coverage.
BIST is fast and on-chip but adds area and aliasing risk.
IP blocks need test access and isolation.
Combine scan, compression, BIST, and JTAG for SoC test.

bank.q: A mixed-signal block is tested for INL, DNL, gain error, offset error, and SINAD. Analyze what each measurement tells and how tolerances are set.
outline: INL is maximum deviation from ideal transfer line.
DNL is deviation of one step from ideal step.
Gain and offset are endpoint errors.
SINAD includes noise and distortion.
Limits come from specification and test guardband.

bank.q: Discuss chip-level and system-level test flow from wafer to board. Include KGD, burn-in, ICT, TAM, and test compression.
outline: Wafer sort tests die before packaging.
Package final test checks assembled chip.
Burn-in screens early failures.
KGD supports multichip assembly.
Board ICT, boundary scan, TAM, and compression reduce system test cost.

glossary.def: A physical imperfection in a fabricated chip.
An incorrect logic value or timing caused by a defect.
A chip or system not meeting its specification.
A logical model of a defect used for test generation.
The fraction of fabricated chips that pass all tests.
A modeled fault where a line is permanently 0 or 1.
A modeled timing fault where a signal arrives too late.
Automatic test pattern generation that derives vectors for faults.
The percentage of modeled faults detected by a test set.
The process of injecting faults and checking which vectors detect them.
A shift register formed by scan flip-flops during test.
A design where every flip-flop is a scan cell.
The ability to set an internal node from primary inputs.
The ability to observe an internal node at primary outputs.
A test method using cells at chip pins to test board connections.
Test access port: the JTAG serial controller and its pins.
Built-in self-test using on-chip pattern generation and checking.
Linear feedback shift register used to generate patterns or compact responses.
An ordered memory test sequence of reads and writes over addresses.
Known-good-die: a die tested before packaging or assembly.
A stress test that screens early-life chip failures.
In-circuit test that checks board components and connections.
Differential nonlinearity: deviation of one converter step from ideal.
Integral nonlinearity: maximum deviation from the ideal converter line.
Quiescent supply current measured to detect defects such as shorts.
